sections.heading: AC and Furnace Trouble in Lincoln, and What to Look For
body: Most no-cooling and no-heat calls come down to one failed part. These are the ones that come up most.

items.title: The air conditioner hums but won't start
items.text: A weak capacitor is a common cause, and it's one of the smaller repairs in the trade.

items.title: The vents blow air that isn't cold
items.text: Low refrigerant points to a leak, and ice on the line points to airflow. Adding refrigerant without finding the leak only delays the next call.

items.title: The furnace clicks but never lights
items.text: Often a worn igniter or a dirty flame sensor. Both are small parts.

items.title: The furnace runs, then shuts itself off
items.text: A clogged filter can make it overheat. A tired sensor can do the same.

items.title: A noise that wasn't there last week
items.text: A squeal or rattle is the system telling you something. Have it looked at while it's still a small job.

tail: If it's one of these, it's a repair. Whether the whole system needs replacing is a different question, and it comes after.

sections.heading: What Usually Goes Wrong With an Air Conditioner
body: A short list of parts accounts for most no-cooling calls. Ice on the refrigerant line, water around the indoor unit, an outdoor fan that isn't spinning or a breaker that trips each time it starts are all signs to stop and call.
If you see ice or water, turn the system off. A struggling air conditioner can turn a small repair into a bigger one.

items.title: A capacitor that's gone weak
items.text: It gives the compressor and the fan motor the jolt to start. When it fades, the unit hums and won't run. This is one of the most common repairs.

items.title: A frozen coil
items.text: A dirty filter or a blocked coil chokes the airflow until ice builds up. Thawing the coil is the easy part, and the repair is finding out why it froze.

items.title: Low refrigerant
items.text: An air conditioner doesn't use refrigerant up, so low means a leak. Topping it off without fixing the leak buys a short break.

items.title: A tired fan or compressor motor
items.text: A motor that's slow or noisy is a warning. Replacing it early is a smaller job than replacing it after it quits.

items.title: A control that isn't telling the unit to run
items.text: A dead thermostat battery or a failed control can look just like a failed air conditioner. It's worth ruling out.

sections.quote: Was so grateful to have my cold air turned on and fixed by just replacing one element and service call for under $200. I was thrilled.

sections.heading: Repair or Replace Your Air Conditioner?
body: Here's a rule you can check. If the problem is a capacitor, a motor or a coil that needs cleaning, repair is the answer, and it costs far less than a new system.
If the unit is old, repairs keep stacking up or the compressor has failed, that's when to price a new one. A large repair bill on an old unit is often money better put toward a replacement.
You'll hear which side you're on, including when the answer is to repair. When it's time to replace, we install and replace air conditioners, with a free estimate first.

body: If you can do it safely, a few checks can save a visit, or at least give us more to go on when you call.
list: The thermostat: is it set to cool, and are the batteries fresh?
The breaker for the outdoor unit: has it tripped?
The filter: if it's gray and packed with dust, change it and give the system an hour.
The outdoor unit: clear away grass, leaves or anything stacked against it.
